glance: An Anthropic mathematician and an NYU colleague claim an AI-written proof that Navier–Stokes flows can blow up on their own, and Italy approves Tesla's supervised driver assistance, bringing it to almost a third of the EU. TSMC pauses some shipments under new US export rules, Leapmotor outsells Tesla in Europe, and Opel buys Leapmotor engineering for a Spanish-built SUV.
brief: The biggest story is mathematical. Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge of Anthropic claim a proof that smooth Navier–Stokes flows can break down in finite time without any outside force, which would settle part of a Millennium Prize problem. Claude wrote the first version of the proof, and it is backed by a huge Lean formalisation, but the key numerical certificate is unpublished and nothing is peer reviewed yet. In Europe, Italy has approved Tesla's supervised driver assistance, the twelfth country to do so, so close to thirty percent of the EU population can now use it. An EU-wide vote has slipped to December at the earliest. TSMC has paused shipments to several chip designers while it checks new US export rules that now cover chips at sixteen nanometres and below. The US Senate voted to make data centres pay for the grid upgrades they cause. Google told schools that Search comes with AI Overviews, and big districts object. ChatGPT Space reached Plus users, with pages that refresh themselves from connected apps. Persona AI's welding humanoids are training in HD Hyundai shipyards. In cars, Leapmotor outsold Tesla in Europe in October. Opel is paying Leapmotor one hundred million euros to engineer an electric SUV for Zaragoza. Tesla began rolling out FSD version fifteen. German politicians want carmakers to keep production at home, and Culina ordered over a thousand Volvo FH Aero trucks. In research, worn seals are shown to hide rotor instability, and a robot eddy current system finds hidden blade defects.

stories.headline: Anthropic and NYU mathematicians claim an AI-written proof that Navier–Stokes flows can blow up without any outside force
stories.why: If it holds, AI will have helped settle a Millennium Prize problem at the heart of every CFD code engineers use.
body: Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge of Anthropic posted a 79-page paper on Friday claiming that smooth solutions to the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations can break down in finite time with no external forcing. The authors say this disproves two of the statements in the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize problem, which carries a one-million-dollar prize. The blow-up rate they find matches a lower bound Jean Leray identified in 1934. A companion paper claims a similar result for the Euler equations.

According to the paper, Claude wrote the first force-free version of the proof, and the authors then rewrote it with help from Claude and OpenAI's Codex. The argument is backed by a Lean 4 formalisation of about 600,000 lines. Important caveats remain: the key numerical certificate has so far been published only as a cryptographic hash, the interval-arithmetic step is not formalised, the code was patched on release day, and there is no peer review yet.
Daily CFD work is unaffected. But it is a strong sign that AI can contribute to deep analysis, and it follows a Claude-assisted Riemann Hypothesis claim by another Anthropic mathematician.

stories.headline: Italy approves Tesla's supervised driver assistance, bringing it to about 30% of the EU population
stories.why: National recognition of a Dutch approval is becoming Europe's route for advanced Level 2 systems while an EU-wide vote stalls.
body: Italy's transport ministry has given provisional approval to Tesla Assisted Driving, the European name for FSD (Supervised), making Italy the twelfth European country to allow it. The approval builds on the Dutch RDW's type approval from April, granted under Article 39 of the EU type-approval regulation, which lets other member states recognise it nationally. With Italy's roughly 59 million people, close to 30% of the EU population can now use the system, about double the share before. Tesla has not given a rollout date.

The system remains SAE Level 2, with the driver responsible at all times. Italy approved the version with the stricter driver monitoring that RDW signed off on 16 November, including hands on the wheel above 130 km/h, and Tesla has cut the allowed speed margin over the limit from 50% to 10%.

An EU-wide approval needs a qualified majority in the TCMV committee, and that vote has slipped to December at the earliest. France has refused, Spain has not recognised the Dutch approval and Sweden is still reviewing it. For ADAS teams, the case shows how far national recognition can stretch type-approval rules.

stories.headline: TSMC pauses shipments to several chip designers as new US export rules reach beyond AI chips
stories.why: Export controls now touch ordinary consumer and automotive-class chips at 16 nm and below, not just AI accelerators.
body: Taiwan's TSMC has held back shipments to several chip developers, both Chinese and non-Chinese, while it reviews compliance with tighter US Commerce Department rules that took effect on Thursday 19 November, Nikkei Asia reported. Under the new rules, foundries must treat chips made at 14/16 nm or more advanced nodes as presumptively restricted unless the designer is on a US-approved list.

The rules also close a route where independent packaging and testing companies certified that a design was not an AI chip and therefore fell outside the controls. Executives told Nikkei the effect spreads to mobile and consumer chips and to designers outside China, while Chinese firms are pushed back towards 28 nm and 40 nm processes.

For automotive buyers the immediate exposure is limited, since many vehicle microcontrollers use older nodes. But ADAS processors, infotainment chips and zone controllers increasingly use advanced nodes, so purchasing and supply-chain teams should check which suppliers' designs are caught by the review.

stories.headline: US Senate votes 62–33 to make data centres pay for the grid upgrades they trigger
stories.why: Power costs for AI computing are becoming a political issue, which will feed into cloud and AI pricing.
body: The US Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act by 62 votes to 33, with fifteen Democrats voting yes. The bill directs the energy regulator FERC to write rules that charge all data centres, new and existing, for the grid upgrades they require and for their use of the existing network. It also speeds up environmental reviews for power lines, solar and wind farms, mines and drilling.

Analysis by Grid Strategies, cited by Senator Martin Heinrich's office, estimates data centres would contribute about 55 billion dollars to transmission costs over ten years, roughly 35 billion more than under current policy. Supporters project household bills falling by 50 to 78 dollars a year by 2040. The bill now goes to the House.

For product teams, the direction matters more than the detail: the energy cost of running AI features is being pushed back onto the operators, and some of it will reach customers through cloud prices.

stories.headline: Google tells schools that keeping Search means keeping AI Overviews, and big US districts push back
stories.why: Bundling AI into a core product with no off switch is meeting resistance from large institutional customers.
body: Google has told schools that its Search product comes with AI Overviews and cannot be separated, Fortune reports. Earlier this month Google reversed course on its Classroom assistant, making Gemini off by default for school student accounts from early 2027 unless administrators switch it on. But Search stays tied to AI summaries, and Google's education vice president said students at schools that ban AI will not have access to search.

Three of the four largest US school districts are resisting. New York City, with about 1.3 million Chromebooks, has disabled Gemini and AI Mode on student devices. Los Angeles has blocked generative AI for about 378,000 students and asked Google for an off switch, and Chicago says it is exploring all options. Alphabet did not comment.

For product managers, it is a clear case of the trade-off between pushing AI adoption through defaults and giving buyers control. Enterprise and public-sector customers increasingly expect admin settings that let them turn individual AI features off.

stories.headline: ChatGPT Space reaches Plus users, with pages and slides that refresh themselves from connected apps
stories.why: Self-updating documents built by an assistant compete directly with dashboards, wikis and slide tools.
body: OpenAI has rolled out ChatGPT Space to Plus subscribers aged 18 and over. Space lets users create interactive pages and presentations, invite collaborators, and set pages and slides to update automatically from connected apps and tools. It replaces the old Library as the home for pages, slides, images and uploaded files, and pages can be edited on the web, desktop and mobile apps. Space first launched for higher tiers at the end of September.
Sharing is restricted: a viewer needs permission and a paid ChatGPT plan with Space. Free users cannot open shared pages, and there are no public links.

For designers and product teams the interesting pattern is the living document: an artefact that an assistant keeps current from live data, rather than a static export. It raises familiar UX questions about provenance and trust, such as showing when content last refreshed and which source changed it. The paid-only sharing model also limits how far such pages can travel outside an organisation.

stories.headline: Persona AI ships welding humanoids to HD Hyundai shipyards, where skilled welders are training them
stories.why: Humanoids are being taught trade skills on existing equipment, a model that could reach heavy fabrication in vehicle plants.
body: US robot maker Persona AI has shipped its bipedal humanoid robots to Korea, where HD Hyundai's shipbuilding and robotics units are developing their welding functions. Skilled welders in the US and Korea are training the robots. The partners signed a development agreement in March, built second-generation robots in May and passed enterprise-grade quality validation in September. Commercial use is expected around the end of the year, with a first site planned.

HD Hyundai is responsible for integration, welding-quality technology and staged rollout. A key design goal is that the robot works with existing welding gear built for people, including a 15 kg wire feeder, rather than needing a rebuilt workcell.

For manufacturing engineers, shipyard welding is a demanding test of mobile robots in unstructured, cramped spaces. If the approach works, similar robots could take on low-volume welding and repair tasks in truck, bus and body-in-white production, where fixed robot cells are hard to justify.

stories.headline: Leapmotor outsells Tesla in Europe in October as Chinese brands double their volume
stories.why: Chinese brands are scaling fast in Europe through Stellantis channels and hybrids, even as their share dips.
body: Preliminary Dataforce figures covering about 98% of the European market show Leapmotor registered 13,902 cars in October, up 256%, ahead of Tesla's 11,722. Tesla's sales are concentrated in the last month of each quarter. The overall market rose 3.3% to about 1.11 million cars, and battery-electric cars grew 57% to a 31% share, while petrol fell 18% and diesel 26%.

Chinese brands more than doubled their combined volume, but their share slipped to 13.5% from a record 14.6% in September. Geely jumped to 8,144 cars and Chery grew 290%. Polestar was the only major Chinese-owned brand to fall, down 30% to 2,659. Chinese brands also registered 52,467 plug-in hybrids, up 182%, likely pulled forward before an EU cap of 350,000 Chinese hybrids a year starts in December.
For European OEMs and suppliers, the numbers show competition now coming through hybrids and partnerships as well as pure EVs. Official ACEA figures follow later this month.

stories.headline: Opel pays Leapmotor 100 million euros to engineer an electric C-SUV for Zaragoza from 2028
stories.why: A European brand is buying a Chinese EV platform and engineering service, a template other OEMs are studying.
body: Opel and Leapmotor have signed the cooperation agreement for a new electric C-segment SUV. Leapmotor will provide engineering and development services for about 100 million euros, according to its Hong Kong stock exchange filing. Production is planned at Stellantis's Zaragoza plant in Spain from September 2028, on a new line shared with the Leapmotor B10.

Leapmotor supplies the EV architecture, battery technology and core components. Opel handles exterior design, ergonomics, chassis engineering, lighting and seats, with joint teams in Rüsselsheim and Hangzhou. Stellantis owns about 20% of Leapmotor, so the deal counts as a connected transaction, and component supply needs a separate agreement. The project was first announced in May with a target of under two years' development.

For engineers, the split is telling: the European side keeps brand-defining work such as chassis tuning and design, while platform, battery and electronics come from China. That shifts where validation and supplier work happen.

stories.headline: Tesla starts rolling out FSD v15 with a new vision encoder and claims 25 times fewer critical interventions
stories.why: A single vision model shared across cars and robots is Tesla's bet for reaching unsupervised driving.
body: Tesla has begun rolling out version 15 of its FSD software in North America. The main change is a new vision encoder, shared across FSD, Robotaxi and the Optimus robot and trained on millions of internet videos. Tesla claims it improves the critical intervention rate by 25 times, but has not published the underlying rate. Electrek's own extrapolation, not a Tesla figure, puts it at around 50,000 miles between critical interventions.

Other changes include a single end-to-end visualisation called Reality View, an end-to-end navigation model, better detection of signs, debris, potholes and standing water, and handling of speed cameras and school zones. Tesla says its current AI4 computer is sufficient.

For ADAS and validation teams, the release highlights a familiar gap: large claimed improvements without public, comparable metrics. A US NHTSA investigation from October 2025 is still open, and European tests have found the system speeding in 30 km/h zones.

stories.headline: German politicians press carmakers to keep development and production at home before VW pay talks
stories.why: Political pressure is rising on OEMs that plan to move work out of Germany, with knock-on effects for suppliers.
body: Federal Transport Minister Steffen Bilger told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung that Germany must remain the home base for vehicle development and production. He called the end of the EU's 2035 combustion-engine ban a political achievement and said carmakers should now commit to German sites in return. He blamed high costs on labour, energy and bureaucracy and called for a European response to subsidised Chinese cars.

Lower Saxony's premier Olaf Lies, who sits on Volkswagen's supervisory board, rejected management's planned job cuts just before VW's pay talks with IG Metall begin on Tuesday. He argued that a German company cannot be saved by giving up production in Germany, and proposed more automation, robotics, better workflows and costs in line with other European plants instead.
For suppliers in Germany and the Nordics, the statements signal that site decisions at VW and others will be politically contested over the coming months, while pay talks and strikes continue.

stories.headline: UK haulier Culina orders 1,051 Volvo FH Aero trucks
stories.why: A large diesel order for Volvo shows fleets still buying efficiency upgrades rather than switching to electric.
body: British logistics group Culina has ordered 1,051 Volvo FH Aero trucks, after putting 134 Volvo FH trucks into service in 2024, Dutch trade magazine NT reports. The trucks will arrive in three batches, with all on the road by the second quarter of 2027, and each is expected to cover between 150,000 and 260,000 kilometres a year.

The order is for diesel trucks with Volvo's D13TC turbo-compound engine, which adds 300 Nm of torque and recovers energy from exhaust gas, combined with the I-Shift automated gearbox and predictive cruise control. The FH Aero's longer, more aerodynamic cab is designed to cut fuel use on long-haul routes.

The order has so far been reported by a single trade source, without a Volvo Group release. For drivetrain engineers it is a reminder that high-mileage diesel powertrains, with their gearbox and bearing loads, will make up a large part of European truck fleets for years, even as electric truck sales grow.

stories.headline: Worn seal teeth can make rotor vibration look better while instability grows, study finds
stories.why: Condition monitoring that only tracks the 1× vibration level may miss a developing rotor–bearing instability.
body: Researchers at the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology and Southeast University in Nanjing studied how mushroom-shaped wear on labyrinth seal teeth changes a rotor running on plain journal bearings. The peer-reviewed paper in Lubricants uses CFD to compute seal stiffness and damping at different wear depths, then feeds these into a finite-element rotor model.

Wear of 0.6 mm raised leakage by about 295%. Effective seal damping fell by 43 to 68%, resonance amplitude grew by 17.8%, and the onset of oil whirl dropped from 3,650 to about 3,530 rpm. At 4,800 rpm, synchronous vibration fell by 27.6% while subsynchronous vibration rose by 39.9%.

The practical point is that a worn seal can make the usual once-per-revolution vibration look healthier while the machine moves closer to instability. Monitoring rules should also track subsynchronous content. The method, feeding component coefficients from CFD into a rotordynamics model, is also a useful pattern for virtual validation of turbomachinery and high-speed e-drive rotors.

stories.headline: Robot-guided eddy current probe designed by simulation finds hidden defects in turbine blades
stories.why: The same simulate-then-automate approach could speed up eddy current inspection of bearing rings, gears and shafts.
body: A team from Nanchang Hangkong University and AECC Power Corporation in Zhuzhou has published a peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Nondestructive Evaluation on automating eddy current inspection of aero-engine turbine blades. They used electromagnetic finite-element simulation to choose the probe's core material and coil design, removing the blind zones seen in manual inspection.

The probe was mounted on a robot with a turntable, and scan paths were tuned on a notched reference specimen to see how robot speed and defect depth and orientation affect the signal. The abstract reports no numbers, but the paper's figures show signal amplitude rising from about 180 to 800 mV as defect depth increases from 0.1 to 0.5 mm, with the best signal-to-noise ratio at 20 mm/s. The system was then validated on real blades with subsurface cold-shut defects.
For bearing and drivetrain plants, it is a practical template: design the probe in simulation, tune scan parameters on reference parts, then automate inspection of curved precision surfaces.

watch.title: Stellantis motorsport cuts
watch.text: Le Figaro reports works-council meetings at Stellantis Motorsport on Monday 23 November, with Peugeot's endurance programme and other racing projects at risk. Not yet confirmed.

watch.title: Battery health display from 29 November
watch.text: Under Euro 7, new car types approved from 29 November must show traction-battery state of health to the driver, for batteries of 2 kWh and up.

watch.title: EU vote on Tesla's system
watch.text: The TCMV committee's vote on EU-wide approval of Tesla's supervised driving has been pushed to December at the earliest; Sweden is still reviewing it.
